title: Controlling Uncertainty: A Review of Human Behavior in Complex Dynamic Environments
authors: Magda Osman, Year not specified in paper (likely 2008-2009 based on citations)
review_question: How do people learn to respond to ill-structured problems in uncertain dynamic environments with shifting goals, feedback loops, time pressures, high stakes, multiple players, and organizational norms, and how can a novel framework integrate diverse research findings on this topic?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly stated as formal criteria; the review synthesizes theoretical developments and empirical work on Complex Dynamic Control (CDC) tasks from diverse domains (Economics, Engineering, Ergonomics, HCI, Management, Psychology).

findings.consequent: Psychological uncertainty (predictability of environment and control)
findings.source: Novel aspects of the MC-Framework, page 27
findings.quote: all CDC tasks generate psychological uncertainty which can be indexed according to: 1) people's subjective confidence in predicting outcomes of events in a CDC task (predictability of the environment), and 2) their expectancy that an action can be executed that will achieve a specific outcome (predictability of control).

findings.consequent: Continuous monitoring (task-monitoring and self-monitoring) of task and goal-directed actions
findings.source: Main tenets of the MC-Framework, page 30-31
findings.quote: High uncertainty will lead to continuous monitoring of the task and goal directed actions

findings.consequent: Periodic monitoring (task-monitoring and self-monitoring) of task and goal-directed actions
findings.source: Main tenets of the MC-Framework, page 30-31
findings.quote: low uncertainty will lead to periodic monitoring of the task and goal directed actions

findings.consequent: Control behaviors (generation of actions)
findings.source: Main tenets of the MC-Framework, page 31
findings.quote: There is a reciprocal relationship between monitoring and control behaviors. The relationship between both types of monitoring behavior and control behavior involves feedforward from monitoring to control, to generate appropriate control behaviors, and feedback to update knowledge of the task, and knowledge of the status between desired and achieved outcomes.

findings.consequent: Reliance on biases (e.g., one-to-one mapping, positive/linear/unidirectional links, immediate effects)
findings.source: Task-Monitoring behaviors, page 32
findings.quote: Biases are assumptions that people make about the behaviour of the task, and are designed to reduce uncertainty by generating hypotheses to test, or for predicting outcomes that are likely to occur

findings.antecedent: Prolonged reliance on biases (under high uncertainty)
findings.consequent: Poor task knowledge and poor control performance
findings.source: Task-Monitoring behaviors, page 33
findings.quote: prolonged reliance on biases leads to poor task knowledge, and poor control.

findings.consequent: Reliance on pattern-matching (to previous experiences)
findings.source: Task-Monitoring behaviors, page 33
findings.quote: pattern-matching is a speedy means of isolating any features of the task that may relate to previous experiences of similar situations

findings.consequent: Inaccurate task knowledge and poor control performance
findings.source: Task-Monitoring behaviors, page 33
findings.quote: if such plans are inappropriate for the current CDC task then inaccurate knowledge of the task develops

findings.consequent: Poor ability to isolate action-outcome associations
findings.source: Self-Monitoring behaviors, page 35
findings.quote: People's ability to successfully isolate action-outcome associations in the task environment is commonly reported to be poor

findings.consequent: Degraded accuracy in recalling action-outcome associations (due to working memory demands)
findings.source: Self-Monitoring behaviors, page 35
findings.quote: accuracy in recalling action-outcome associations is also degraded, because of the high demands placed on working memory at the time in which the individual experiences uncertainty

findings.consequent: High accuracy of detection and recall of action-outcome associations
findings.source: Self-Monitoring behaviors, page 35
findings.quote: Studies in which high accuracy of detection and recall of action-outcome associations is demonstrated

findings.consequent: Continual monitoring of behaviors (task-monitoring, self-monitoring)
findings.source: Relationship between Monitoring (...) and control, page 36
findings.quote: difficulty in organizing plans of action designed to reduce the discrepancy between one's current and desired goals leads continual monitoring of behaviors

findings.consequent: Poor resource allocation (e.g., attention, cognitive effort)
findings.source: Relationship between Monitoring (...) and control, page 36
findings.quote: Often, resource allocation is not well calibrated to the task

findings.consequent: Lack of relationship between performance and effort
findings.source: Relationship between Monitoring (...) and control, page 36
findings.quote: there is often no relationship between performance and effort

findings.antecedent: Low psychological uncertainty (familiar environment, practiced actions)
findings.consequent: Less frequent alternation between monitoring and control behaviors
findings.source: Relationship between Monitoring (...) and control, page 37
findings.quote: The alternation between monitoring (task-monitoring, self-monitoring) and control behaviors is less frequent when the individual judges the environment to be sufficiently familiar to draw on highly practiced plans of actions

findings.consequent: Reduced attention to feedback from actions and decisions
findings.source: Relationship between Monitoring (...) and control, page 37
findings.quote: other behaviors that have been commonly reported under these conditions include reduced attention to feedback from the actions and decisions taken

findings.consequent: Degraded control performance and errors in judgment (similar to novices)
findings.source: New Insights into Old Issues - Experts vs. Novices, page 40
findings.quote: under conditions judged highly uncertain, experts can fall into the same traps as novices, and return to default-based assumptions or make errors in judgment, and their control performance degrades much in the same way as novices.

findings.consequent: Control performance in CDC tasks
findings.source: New Insights into Old Issues - Cognitive ability, page 41
findings.quote: control performance may be more accurately indexed by perceived estimates of uncertainty rather than of cognitive ability

findings.antecedent: Maintenance of psychological uncertainty (regardless of practice)
findings.consequent: Improvements in control behaviors
findings.source: New Insights into Old Issues - Practice effects, page 41
findings.quote: Regardless of practice, if experiences of uncertainty are maintained, then no improvements in control behaviors will be observed.

findings.antecedent: Prevention of concurrent monitoring behaviors during learning (e.g., avoiding hypothesis testing, lack of information to track decisions/outcomes)
findings.consequent: Dissociation between procedural and declarative knowledge
findings.source: New Insights into Old Issues - Dissociable mechanisms, page 42
findings.quote: Common to studies that have shown dissociations between procedural and declarative knowledge in CDC tasks is the prevention of monitoring behaviors designed to evaluate action-outcomes and input-output associations.

findings.antecedent: Reciprocal relationship between agency and causality (as proposed by MC framework)
findings.consequent: People's ability to control outcomes in CDC tasks and their causal understanding
findings.source: Agency and Causality, page 44
findings.quote: The interpretation of the relationship between causality and agency offered by the MC framework is that it is reciprocal, in that people treat the task environment as an uncertain one, and that, if there are factors contributing to dissonance between the predicted and actual outcomes, this will further reduce people's sense of agency which is a reflection of their ability to control the outcome in the CDC task and uncertainty, and disrupt their causal understanding

findings.antecedent: High judgments of self-efficacy (as an index of agency)
findings.consequent: Successful identification of causal structures, better control performance, and further increases in self-efficacy
findings.source: Agency and Causality, page 45
findings.quote: Osman (2008a) revealed that high judgments of self-efficacy in turn led to the successful identification of causal structures in the CDC task, and to better control performance, which in turn lead to further increases in self-efficacy.

findings.consequent: Disrupted perception of self-generated actions and outcomes, impaired control performance, impaired causal knowledge, and further reduced self-efficacy
findings.source: Agency and Causality, page 45
findings.quote: low judgments of self-efficacy disrupted the way in which self-generated actions and their outcomes were perceived. Control performance suffered, and causal knowledge of the system was impaired, and further reduced the subsequent judgments of self-efficacy.

findings.antecedent: Long delays in experiencing effects from actions (in CDC tasks)
findings.consequent: Reduced expectancies of effects, interpretation of system as unpredictable, and undermined sense of agency
findings.source: Agency and Causality, page 45
findings.quote: long delays in experiencing effects from actions generated in the task are difficult to integrate, and so people reduce their expectancies of the effects because they have not been immediately experienced (...) Consequently when the delayed effects are actually experienced, people interpret them as resulting from an unpredictable system, and so they reduce their expectancies of controlling it which undermines their sense of agency

findings.antecedent: Congruence between predicted and actual outcome of one's actions
findings.consequent: Sense of agency
findings.source: Agency and Causality, page 46
findings.quote: our sense of agency depends strongly on the degree to which there is congruence between the predicted and actual outcome of one's actions

synthesis_conclusions: Complex Dynamic Control (CDC) tasks are inherently uncertain environments, and human behavior within them is guided by subjective judgments of this uncertainty.
The Monitoring and Control (MC) framework proposes that psychological uncertainty mediates monitoring behaviors (task-monitoring and self-monitoring), which in turn affect control behaviors.
There is a reciprocal relationship between monitoring and control behaviors, involving both feedforward (generating actions) and feedback (updating knowledge) mechanisms.

Different theoretical accounts of CDC tasks (instance-learning, hypothesis-testing, self-regulation, expert adaptive decision-making, computational) can be integrated by considering their common focus on reducing uncertainty.
Expertise in CDC tasks involves a shift from inefficient processing to fluently reducing uncertainty, but experts can still fall into novice traps under high uncertainty.
The relationship between agency and causality is reciprocal: uncertainty disrupts causal understanding and sense of agency, while high self-efficacy enhances both.
evidence_gaps: Formal descriptions of the CDC task environment are often lacking in theoretical accounts, making it difficult to bridge the gap between modeling the environment and skilled human behavior.
There is a need to explore how people develop and adapt their causal models online while interacting with dynamic environments, and how this impacts their sense of agency (and vice versa).
A synthesis of causal structure learning research and CDC tasks research is needed to formally describe human behavior in complex dynamic environments.
limitations: The review acknowledges that defining complexity in CDC tasks based solely on objective task characteristics has not always been a successful predictor of performance, suggesting that psychological factors also play a significant role.

The field has mixed findings regarding the relationship between cognitive ability (IQ) and CDC task performance, which the MC framework attempts to explain through subjective experiences of uncertainty.

The review notes that limited training in laboratory CDC tasks often maintains people's experiences of uncertainty, and extended practice alone does not reliably lead to improved performance if uncertainty is not addressed.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans actively regulate their cognitive states and actions to reduce discrepancies between desired and perceived environmental states, thereby controlling uncertainty.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Cognitive Theories of Decision Making Under Uncertainty
theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper synthesizes various cognitive models explaining how individuals perceive, evaluate, and respond to uncertain information in complex dynamic environments.
Uncertainty is presented as a significant stressor in complex dynamic environments, leading to various coping strategies and potential performance decrements.
